finding.claim: Unauthenticated remote Marshal.load of request-supplied data (HIGH; initially CRITICAL, downgraded under triage Check 13 because no gadget chain is confirmed for the deployed gem set). The route also returns state.inspect, which gives attacker feedback.
finding.source: params[:state] on POST /restore (app.rb:6), attacker-controlled, no authentication

trace.note: post "/restore" route accepts any POST, no auth filter
Base64.decode64 decodes attacker bytes with no validation
Marshal.load deserializes the attacker object graph (sink)
state.inspect returns the resulting object representation to the client

finding.guards_checked: No authentication or authorization filter in app.rb; no input validation or type check; Sinatra default Rack::Protection does not address deserialization; deployment controls (WAF, ingress, bind address) unknown; Sinatra default public bind means the loopback downgrade does not apply. Re-score to CRITICAL if a working gadget chain is confirmed in the deployed bundle.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.rb has no authentication, authorization, or input validation between the route and the sink. Line 5 is a bare `post "/restore"` route, and line 6 passes `params[:state]` straight through `Base64.decode64` into `Marshal.load`. The directory holds only app.rb and skill docs: no Gemfile, config.ru, or ingress/WAF config, so no deployment-level control can be confirmed. Sinatra's default Rack::Protection does not filter deserialization payloads.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: app.rb:5 is an unauthenticated POST route, app.rb:6 runs Marshal.load on attacker-supplied decoded bytes with no guard, and app.rb:7 returns state.inspect as feedback. Marshal.load on untrusted input is the dangerous sink itself, so the finding stands regardless of whether a gadget chain exists in the deployed bundle; that only affects severity (the candidate's HIGH rating looks reasonable), and deployment bind address and ingress are unverifiable from this directory.

finding.claim: Reflected HTML injection in /import response via unescaped JSON object keys (MEDIUM; initially HIGH, downgraded because the attack needs a lured victim and Sinatra default Rack::Protection HttpOrigin may block cross-site POSTs).
finding.source: JSON object keys in request body on POST /import (app.rb:11), attacker-controlled
finding.sink: data.keys.join(",") at app.rb:12, returned unescaped with Sinatra default Content-Type text/html

trace.note: data.keys attacker-chosen key strings (Hash only; arrays or scalars raise NoMethodError)
join(",") is the unescaped HTML sink

finding.guards_checked: No output encoding; no explicit Content-Type set; Sinatra default Rack::Protection HttpOrigin is enabled unless disabled and is not configured in app.rb, so it may reject cross-origin POSTs; not verified at runtime. Attack requires a victim browser driven to a cross-site form POST.

verdict.guard_found: Sinatra's default Rack::Protection stack, including HttpOrigin, which is not disabled in app.rb (no `set :protection` or `disable :protection` anywhere in app.rb:1-17). Browsers send an Origin header on cross-site form POSTs, and HttpOrigin rejects a mismatched Origin with 403 before the route runs at app.rb:10-12. I did not run the app to confirm the framework default.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (app.rb:10 route, app.rb:11 attacker-controlled JSON body, app.rb:12 keys joined and returned as text/html), but exploitation needs a victim browser to send a cross-site POST, which Sinatra's default HttpOrigin protection blocks since app.rb does not disable protection, so the effective control defeats the claimed attack path.
